payload.title: Token rewards and homework completion
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original source — a summary of a (fictional) peer-reviewed study.

Token Rewards and Homework Completion in Fifth Graders

Introduction
Teachers want students to finish their homework regularly. Behavioral research suggests that reinforcing a behavior makes it more likely to occur. In this study, researchers tested the hypothesis that fifth graders who earn tokens for completing homework will complete a greater percentage of their homework than fifth graders who earn no tokens.

Participants
The 100 participants were fifth graders from four classrooms in one public elementary school. All students whose parents returned a permission form and who agreed to take part were included. A computer randomly assigned the students to the Token group (50 students) or the No-token group (50 students).

Procedure
For six weeks, teachers assigned the same daily homework to all students. In the Token group, a student earned one token for each assignment that was handed in complete, and ten tokens could be exchanged for a classroom privilege. Students in the No-token group received no tokens. Homework completion was defined as the percentage of the assigned homework handed in complete during the six weeks.

Ethical procedures
The school district's institutional review board approved the study. Parents gave written permission, and each student agreed and was told that he or she could stop at any time without penalty. At the end of the study, the No-token group was also offered the token program. Students' records were identified only by code numbers.

Results
The table shows the results. The researchers reported that the difference between the groups was statistically significant.

payload.title: Social support and perceived stress
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original source — a summary of a (fictional) peer-reviewed study.

Social Support and Perceived Stress in First-Year College Students

Introduction
The first year of college can be stressful. Health psychologists have proposed that people who feel supported by others cope better with stress. This study tested the hypothesis that first-year students who report more social support report less perceived stress.

Participants
The 150 participants were first-year students at one university. The researchers emailed a link to the survey to 900 first-year students, and the 150 students who completed it were included in the study.

Procedure
Each student completed an online survey once, in the middle of the fall semester. Social support was defined as the student's total score on a 10-item questionnaire about how much help and encouragement the student receives from friends and family (scores from 10 to 50). Perceived stress was defined as the student's total score on a 10-item questionnaire about how overwhelmed the student felt during the past month (scores from 10 to 50).

Ethical procedures
A university institutional review board approved the study. Students read a consent statement before beginning the survey and could close the survey at any time. Survey answers were stored under code numbers, and the researchers did not collect students' names.

Results
The researchers calculated a correlation coefficient between social support scores and perceived stress scores. The table shows the results.

payload.title: Later school start times
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original sources — summaries of three (fictional) peer-reviewed studies.

Source 1: A laboratory experiment on sleep and attention
Researchers randomly assigned 60 high school students to spend either six hours or eight hours in bed for three nights. On the fourth morning, all students completed a 30-minute attention task in which they pressed a key when a target appeared among distractors. The mean accuracy was 71 percent for the six-hour group (30 students) and 85 percent for the eight-hour group (30 students). The difference was statistically significant.

Source 2: A survey of students in two districts
Researchers surveyed 1,200 high school students about their sleep. Students in the district whose school day began at 7:15 a.m. (600 students) reported an average of 6.4 hours of sleep on school nights. Students in the district whose school day began at 8:45 a.m. (600 students) reported an average of 7.6 hours. The researchers noted that the districts were not assigned to start times and may differ in other ways, such as family income.

Source 3: A comparison of grades before and after a schedule change
Researchers followed one school that moved its start time from 7:15 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. The mean grade-point average of the students was 2.90 in the year before the change and 3.02 in the year after. The researchers reported that the difference was not statistically significant (p = .18) and noted that the school also changed some course offerings in the same year.

payload.title: Hiding like counts
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original sources — summaries of three (fictional) peer-reviewed studies.

Source 1: A field experiment with teenagers
Researchers randomly assigned 100 teenagers to use a photo-sharing app for two weeks in one of two versions. In the Visible version (50 teenagers), like counts were shown under each post. In the Hidden version (50 teenagers), like counts were not shown. At the end of two weeks, each teenager rated how worried he or she felt about how others viewed his or her posts on a scale from 1 to 10. The mean rating was 6.8 in the Visible version and 5.2 in the Hidden version. The difference was statistically significant.

Source 2: A survey of teenage app users
Researchers surveyed 800 teenagers. Teenagers who said they check the like counts on their posts more than ten times a day reported lower self-esteem, and the correlation between how often teenagers check like counts and self-esteem was r = -0.31. The researchers noted that teenagers who volunteered for the survey may differ from teenagers who did not.

Source 3: Interviews with teenagers about hidden counts
Researchers interviewed 30 teenagers whose app had hidden like counts for one month. Of the 30, 19 said that they felt less pressure to post only popular photos. Eleven said that they still worried about what others thought of their posts and found other ways to compare themselves, such as counting comments. The researchers noted that teenagers who agreed to be interviewed may have had stronger opinions than others.
